questions.text: The supplied HEA notes describe high-entropy alloys as alloys containing:

options.label: a
options.text: One base element with trace additions only

options.label: b
options.text: Five or more principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions

options.label: c
options.text: Exactly two elements in equal proportions

questions.detailed: The notes define HEAs as combining five or more principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions, typically with each principal element in a broad 5–35 at.% range.

questions.text: The ideal configurational entropy of an equimolar random alloy containing $n$ components is:
questions.detailed: For random mixing, $\Delta S_{conf}=-R\sum_i x_i\ln x_i$. In an equimolar alloy, $x_i=1/n$, giving $\Delta S_{conf}=-R\ln(1/n)=R\ln n$.

questions.text: Calculate the ideal molar configurational entropy of a five-component equimolar alloy using $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$.
According to the supplied notes, the high-entropy classification threshold is approximately:
questions.detailed: The HEA notes state that an alloy is generally classified as high entropy when its configurational entropy of mixing exceeds $1.5R$. A five-element equimolar alloy has $R\ln5\approx1.61R$.

questions.text: A five-component equimolar alloy has $\Delta H_{mix}=5.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta S_{mix}=1.61R$. Estimate $\Delta G_{mix}$ at 1000 K using $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$.
questions.detailed: Use $\Delta G_{mix}=\Delta H_{mix}-T\Delta S_{mix}$. Here $\Delta S=1.61(8.314)=13.38\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Thus $\Delta G=5000-1000(13.38)=-8380\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\approx-8.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: Why can increasing temperature favour a random solid solution in an HEA with positive enthalpy of mixing?

options.label: a
options.text: The $-T\Delta S_{mix}$ term becomes more negative and can offset positive $\Delta H_{mix}$

options.label: d
options.text: The equilibrium constant becomes independent of temperature

questions.detailed: The mixing free energy is $\Delta G_{mix}=\Delta H_{mix}-T\Delta S_{mix}$. A large positive configurational entropy makes the entropic contribution increasingly stabilizing as temperature rises, potentially offsetting a positive enthalpy of mixing.

questions.text: Short-range chemical order in an HEA means:

options.label: a
options.text: Every atom has a perfectly random neighbourhood

options.label: b
options.text: Local atomic arrangements show preferred correlations even when the alloy is not long-range ordered

options.label: c
options.text: The alloy has no configurational entropy

questions.detailed: The supplied HEA notes caution that perfect randomness is an idealization. Chemical short-range order (CSRO) describes preferred local atomic correlations and can be deliberately tuned rather than treated simply as a defect.

questions.text: The sluggish-diffusion effect in HEAs is classified primarily as a:

options.label: b
options.text: Kinetic effect that can slow phase transformations

options.label: d
options.text: Change in the universal gas constant

questions.detailed: The notes identify sluggish diffusion as a kinetic effect. A complex local chemical environment can raise or spatially vary migration barriers, slowing atomic transport and some phase transformations.

questions.text: Which combination correctly pairs the HEA core effects with their broad roles?

options.label: c
options.text: All four effects are exclusively thermodynamic

options.label: d
options.text: All four effects are exclusively mechanical

questions.detailed: The supplied notes distinguish the high-entropy effect as thermodynamic, sluggish diffusion as kinetic, and severe lattice distortion as structural. The cocktail effect refers to the combined property response of multiple principal elements.

questions.text: Why does high configurational entropy alone not guarantee a single-phase HEA?

options.label: a
options.text: Phase stability also depends on enthalpy and other material-specific factors

options.label: b
options.text: Entropy is unrelated to Gibbs energy

options.label: c
options.text: A single phase requires zero temperature

questions.detailed: The notes explicitly caution that entropy alone does not guarantee a single-phase solid solution. The phase selection depends on the total Gibbs energy, including enthalpic interactions and other factors; empirical design rules are therefore also used.
